name: Solomon Islands

findings.local_actor: Solomon Islands government (Solomon Island Submarine Cable Company)
findings.reversal_of: 2017 agreement with Huawei Marine to build the Solomon Islands international submarine cable (Sydney landing)
findings.summary: After the Solomons agreed a cable deal with Huawei in 2017, Australia, citing security concerns, refused it a Sydney landing; Vocus, on Australia's behalf, replaced Huawei and the Australia-funded Coral Sea Cable was built instead.
findings.analyst_inference: Tier 3 assumes the 2017 Huawei agreement was a signed contract (iTWire: contract 'awarded'; ODT: deal 'agreed'); value undisclosed. Dated to the January 2018 Vocus replacement; the decision itself was late 2017. Still current: SubTel Forum (2021) reports the Australian-built system was completed in 2019.

findings.controller: Alcatel Submarine Networks (then part of Nokia)
findings.local_actor: Solomon Island Submarine Cable Company Ltd (government-owned)
findings.financier: Australian Government, DFAT (A$91m, about two-thirds of cost)
findings.summary: The Coral Sea Cable system, about 4,700 km linking Sydney with Papua New Guinea and Honiara, was completed in 2019; Australia paid most of the cost, Vocus delivered it and Alcatel Submarine Networks laid the cable.
findings.analyst_inference: Equipment vendor ASN, so pole third (French/Finnish at the time), though the financier and builder are Australian; a reviewer may weigh the Australian funder and Vocus operating role. ODT names Vocus as cable operator; the Solomons landing is held by the state-owned SISCC. A$91m is funding for the whole PNG-Solomons system, not converted, and not a Solomons-only value. Current operating status not checked this run.

findings.local_actor: Ministry of Communication and Aviation (Solomon Islands National Broadband Infrastructure Project)
findings.financier: Export-Import Bank of China (20-year loan at 1%)
findings.summary: The government borrowed from China Exim to build 161 Huawei mobile broadband towers nationwide with CHEC, despite a KPMG warning of losses; by July 2025 about 40 sites were on air, with completion targeted for 2026.

sources.publisher: Office of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, Solomon Islands Government

findings.analyst_inference: Tier 4: loan closed and sites partly operational (about 40 of 161 by July 2025, per state broadcaster SIBC), not yet at scale. Value left null because sources conflict: DCD gives CNY 449m reported as about US$96m, RFA US$65m, a search title US$66m. Operating operator not named in any opened source; Huawei is the equipment vendor, so pole prc.

findings.reversal_of: Malaita's share (27 towers) of the China Exim-financed Huawei national tower rollout
findings.summary: Malaita's provincial assembly refused the 27 Huawei towers planned for the province, citing the Auki Communiqué banning Chinese-funded projects after the 2019 switch from Taiwan to Beijing; sites in Malaita later went on air.
findings.analyst_inference: RFA/BenarNews is US-government funded, so treated as S4; reviewer may rate it S3. still_current false: the China-sceptic premier was ousted in February 2023 (search title only) and an undated SIBC item reports SINBIP sites on air in Malaita, so the refusal appears to have lapsed.

findings.controller: Chinese police (PRC police liaison team in Solomon Islands)
findings.summary: Chinese police piloted China's Fengqiao village-monitoring model in Fighter 1 near Honiara, collecting fingerprints, palm prints and household data, with plans to expand nationally; it was also promoted in 16 Malaita villages.
findings.analyst_inference: Pilot so tier 2. Both opened sources trace to one Reuters report and neither is S1/S2, so not corroborated. No technology vendor, camera system or data-storage location is named; pole prc because Chinese police run the collection. Reviewer may judge this a policing practice rather than an AI-stack application. Builds on the 2022 security pact and 2023 policing agreement.
